extracted.intended_audience: science communicators, institutional press officers, university PR staff, researchers involved in public communication
extracted.subtask_description: A release-level rubric, grounded in NASEM's evidence synthesis, for crafting or assessing science press releases so they are effective, trustworthy, and pickup-worthy across audiences and information ecosystems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align strategy with goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The release must declare (internally) which goal it serves: sharing findings, building appreciation, increasing knowledge of an issue, influencing opinion or behavior, or eliciting public input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases that conflate goals communicate poorly. Internally specifying the intended goal helps determine message framing, evidence emphasis, and evaluation metrics. Avoid writing as if a single release should simultaneously inform, persuade, and solicit public input without clear prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messages to specific audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Different versions or framings are needed for general public, scientists, media, advocacy groups, corporations, health professionals, government agencies, science enthusiasts, policy makers, political commentators, and individual activists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NASEM explicitly rejects one-size-fits-all releases. Identify target audiences and adapt language, level of technical detail, values-based framing, and channels accordingly. Consider creating separate audience-specific summaries rather than one generic release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deal honestly with complexity and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases should not paper over scientific uncertainty; they should communicate it in ways the audience can use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language that signals epistemic status (e.g., 'an early-stage finding,' 'subject to replication,' 'consistent with but not yet proving X'). Avoid overstating certainty or simplifications that mislead audiences about robustness of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go beyond the deficit model
rubrics_metrics.description: The deficit model assumes the audience needs facts and will then agree. NASEM's evidence rejects this: communication must engage values, identities, and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases should not assume that 'if we explain the science, opposition will end.' Design messages that acknowledge audience values and social contexts; pair information with engagement strategies rather than relying solely on factual explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame issues so audiences are receptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame choice (per Hallahan, Kahan) should reflect audience values rather than the scientist's internal frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select frames that align with target audiences' concerns and values to increase receptivity. Test alternative frames when possible; avoid defaulting to technical or discipline-centric frames that may be ignored or resisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize complexity of communication processes (systems approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A release is one node in a system: scientist → PR office → release → wire → reporter → editor → reader → social media → repeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate the full chain and how content may be transformed at each node. Design headlines, quotes, and boilerplate to survive truncation, translation, and paraphrase along distribution pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation built in
rubrics_metrics.description: NASEM recommends communications efforts include planned evaluation. Each release should specify success criteria before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define measurable success criteria in advance (e.g., clip count, sentiment, downstream policy outcomes, public-survey shifts). Plan for collecting metrics and assessing whether the release met its stated goal(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural-cognition awareness (for contentious topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases on topics with known cultural-cognition divides (climate, vaccines, GMO, AI) should test the frame against multiple cultural worldviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how different cultural groups will interpret messages. Pre-test frames and messages across worldview spectra to reduce backfire and improve resonance among diverse audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust-building over persuasion (for contentious topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: NASEM evidence: trust accrues over repeated honest communication. A single release should not aim to convert; it should sustain trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize transparency, acknowledgement of uncertainty, and consistency over time. Use a long-term trust strategy rather than attempting one-off persuasion in a single release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information ecosystem awareness (for contentious topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The release lives in a contested information ecosystem. NASEM advises content that is robust to mis-quotation and stands up under partial reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft messages, quotes, and summaries so that truncated or reworded versions still convey intended meaning and guardrails. Anticipate potential misquotation and design language to minimize distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder participation (for contentious topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: For contentious topics, NASEM endorses including affected community voices in the release rather than only scientist voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involve representatives of affected communities, practitioners, or stakeholders in quotes and framing to increase legitimacy and reduce perceptions of one-sidedness. This supports trust and contextualizes findings within lived experience or policy implications.
